newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: NATO's Solana seeks deal with ex-communists by July.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana seeks deal with ex-communists by July.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said late on Wednesday he aimed to create a new partnership with the former communist states before a controversial NATO summit in Madrid this July.

"We are trying to construct before the month of July what we will call the Atlantic Partnership Council in which we are going to put together the ideas and projects that we have now within the Partnership for Peace programme," Solana told reporters on arrival in the Uzbek capital Tashkent.

Solana is on a whistle-stop tour of four Central Asian nations in an attempt to convince these ex-Soviet states that NATO's sparring with the Kremlin over its planned eastward enlargement does not threaten stability in their own countries.
Moscow and NATO are battling over the alliance's intention to offer membership invitations at the Madrid summit. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first new entrants.

"This will be a flexible programme," Solana said. "Every country will be able to take as much as it wants of this project and we hope this will give an impulse to the relations with the countries with which we cooperate now," he said.
Solana, who is scheduled to meet Uzbek President Islam Karimov on Thursday, gave no further details of the new partnership plan.
Some 27 countries across Europe have now signed up to Partnership for Peace, or PFP, which was created in 1994 to fill the security vacuum following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
NATO wants a revamped and reinvigorated PFP to become a permanent feature of Europe's post-Cold War security system.
But PFP members like Kazakhsan and Kyrgyzstan have already told Solana this week that they fear Russian anger at NATO expansion could jeopardise regional security.
Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev told Solana on Wednesday that he shared Russian worries over the Western defence alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
"We share Russian concerns about NATO enlargement," Akayev said. "Russia is our strategic partner," he added.
Western diplomats say that Central Asia, physically far from Europe, is also far from NATO's main sphere of interest.
The Central Asian republics themselves remain dependent on Moscow, particularly for energy exports, and are careful to be on good terms with the Kremlin.
Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, however, plan to hold a joint 10-day peacekeeping exercise with NATO in the region in September.
Solana can expect a warmer welcome from Uzbekistan's Karimov who, eager for strong ties with the United States, has said he has no problems with NATO expansion eastwards.
